#2853. Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says central bank 'has definitely got work to do' on inflation

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee expressed concern about the latest inflation data, telling CNBC on Friday that the central bank likely will need to take action.

"I believe that the the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility," the policymaker said during an interview on "Squawk Box."

His remarks came shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index, considered a proxy for wholesale prices, posted a 0.3% increase in October, which was slightly less than expected, but also indicated a 6.5% annual gain, the highest since November 2022.

With data in hand earlier in the week showing that the consumer price index rose a bit more than expected during the month, Goolsbee said the Fed is slipping further away from its 2% inflation target.

"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," he said.

"Inflation is rising. It's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks, and now we're adding this old-fashioned demand overheating coming from the AI data center buildout, that looks like it's starting to spread out of its lane," Goolsbee added.

Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase when the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next on Dec. 8-9. There also is a better than 10% probability of a half-point hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures markets. Goolsbee is not currently an FOMC voter but will be in 2027.

Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would entertain a 50 basis point move depending on this week's inflation data.

Goolsbee did not speculate directly on whether the Fed might need to be more aggressive.

"It's it's all going to be about this ... question: What is happening to inflation, and are we on path back to 2%?" he said. "My feeling is, right now we're not."

#2851. Arrowhead Pride Midseason Awards: The Chiefs’ Special Teams MVP

There are eight games in the books — with nine more to go. The Kansas City Chiefs' 2026 season reaches its midpoint in Week 10. Because the team's bye came so early in Week 5, we have decided to move our annual awards to midseason.

Nine members of the Arrowhead Pride writing staff each had one vote for our seven midseason awards, so nine votes will be tallied for each award.

Most Improved Player: DB Chris Roland-Wallace

In this post, we'll reveal the top special teams player:

VOTING: Matt Araiza (8), James Winchester (1)

On some NFL squads, special teams could feel like an afterthought. In Kansas City, a strong tradition of explosive kick and punt returns has changed the team's fortunes. The Chiefs have also boasted some of the best kickers and punters in the league over the past 30 years– along with some of the most painful missed field goals in NFL history.

Expectations are always high for the third phase in KC, as evidenced by the influence and stature of special teams coordinator Dave Toub. It's certainly been an up-and-down season (or two, or three) for Uncle Dave's group, making this a challenging operation to evaluate– or even understand. They've got a struggling kicker, a controversial kicker on the practice squad, and have a number of costly penalties seemingly every week.

We could choose a special teams player of the year in 2026 via process of elimination.

Nobody has stood out as a star on coverage ( they've been fine)

James Winchester is a solid long snapper (but it's hard to judge his impact on a game)

That really only leaves two viable options: Emmett Johnson– who has just started to come on as a kick returner OR punter Matt Araiza, who is statistically among the league leaders at his position this year.

Through eight games, Araiza has punted 25 times for 1,270 yards, averaging 50.8 yards per punt. His longest punt of the season is a 69-yard boot, and he's placed 12 punts inside the 20-yard line.

His AFC Special Teams Player of the Week performance came in the Week 4 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders. Araiza punted five times, and all five landed inside the 20-yard line– most impressive was the one downed at the Raiders' 1-yard line by Xavier Nwankpa and Emmett Johnson. But Araiza's fake punt on the first drive of the game, converting on a 4th and 4 from their own 35, is the play that we'll all remember (even if the offense did nothing with it, turning it over on downs at the 50).

The punter formerly known as "punt god" was known for highlight reel bombs in college. But, Araiza has apparently worked hard to be a complete player at his position. He's improved his touch and directional kicking, resulting in a career-best yards-per-punt average thus far.

Is Araiza the Chiefs' most valuable special teams player through the first half of the season? Let us know in the comments.

#2848. Packers Film Room: How Green Bay racked up interceptions

The Green Bay Packers defense generated three interceptions with sound coverage and defense in Week 9. None came with pressure on the quarterback. In fact, all three of the New England Patriots' quarterback Drake Maye's interceptions against Green Bay came from a clean pocket. The Packers never sent more than four rushers and never blitzed, yet Maye still threw three balls to a defender who was already waiting for them. What ties the picks together is what happened after the snap.

Each time, a Green Bay safety ended up somewhere Maye didn't expect, and Maye threw to the picture he had before the snap. On the first, the single-high safety didn't bite on play action.

On the second, Evan Williams was rotating over the top of what looked like one-on-one coverage. On the third, a deep-quarter safety read Maye's eyes and drove on the dig. Together, the three throws cost New England about 12.4 EPA, and two of them set up Packers touchdowns.

The first interception came on Maye's first pass of the game, on 2nd and 9 from the New England 26 with 14:32 left in the first quarter. Xavier McKinney picked it off at the 50 and returned it 36 yards to the NE 14, and Jordan Love scrambled in for a touchdown two plays later.

At minus 5.90 EPA, it was the costliest of New England's three interceptions. Green Bay was in a drop-8 Cover 3, rushing three with seven in the box. Before the snap, McKinney was the lone deep defender in the middle, about 12 yards off the ball, so the middle of the field was closed. New England ran play action from under center with a deep post and a deep crosser.

That combination is built to stress the post safety. If he carries the post, the crosser opens underneath him, and if he jumps the crosser, the post is open behind him. McKinney never took the fake. He kept his depth and stayed square in the middle third through Maye's drop, so the play action never created the conflict it was designed to.

With eight defenders in coverage, the underneath zones were full, and neither deep route had an easy window. Maye's eyes and shoulders stayed locked on the deep middle, McKinney read him the whole way, and when Maye threw the crosser 24 yards downfield, McKinney broke downhill and caught it in stride around the 50.

Play action against drop-8 Cover 3 only works if the post safety bites. McKinney didn't, so the ball went straight to the defender the concept was meant to beat. With only three rushers and a clean pocket, Maye had time to come off the deep routes and check the ball down. Charting graded it interception-worthy, with a CPOE of minus 42.

The second interception came on 1st and 10 from the New England 40 with 12:54 left in the second quarter. Maye took a deep shot down the left sideline to Kyle Williams, 37 air yards, and Brandon Cisse batted it into the air for Evan Williams to catch at the Green Bay 23. It was the only one of the three the Packers didn't score off, since they went three-and-out, and it cost minus 2.82 EPA.

Green Bay ran a WASP quads pressure with McKinney as the fourth rusher, rotating the coverage behind him. WASP usually puts a linebacker in as the 4th rusher while dropping a defensive end. On this play, McKinney is aligned more like that inside linebacker, so he's the one tasked with adding to the rush.

New England lined up in a shotgun 3×1, with a dagger concept to the trips side and Kyle Williams isolated as the X to the boundary.

Dagger uses a clear-out seam from the inside receiver and a deep dig from the outside receiver into the space the seam vacates. Before the snap, the shell looked two-high, and McKinney gave no clear sign he was coming. At the snap, he rushed, and Evan Williams rotated toward the boundary and got depth over the top of the single-receiver side.

Instead of working the dagger to the trips side, Maye took the backside shot. Cisse was in phase on the go route and Williams was closing from above, so the ball landed between them. Cisse got a hand on it at the sideline, and Williams, already overhead, caught the tip. The backside go is usually a decision made before the snap: one-on-one to the X with no safety help is a throw you take.

Here, though, the safety help only appeared after the snap as Williams rotated over. With a safety rushing, there were also fewer defenders underneath, so the dagger dig and the vacated middle were the coverage's weak spots. The Packers defense made it a contested catch because Maye put too much air under it when it should have been more on a line out to the sideline. Instead, he threw a 50/50 ball into a rotating safety.

The third interception came on 2nd and 7 from the Green Bay 44 with 5:47 left in the second quarter. Maye threw a backside dig to tight end Eli Raridon and McKinney undercut it at the Green Bay 29 and returned it for 2 yards. Christian Watson's 43-yard catch and a Kaleb Johnson touchdown run followed, making it 24-7, and the play cost minus 3.68 EPA.

Green Bay was in Cover 4 "trix," a quarters variation where the weak safety reads the inside receiver from the #3 in trips. The Packers rushed four with no blitz and six in the box, and both safeties sat 12 to 15 yards deep before the snap, with McKinney on the side the ball went to. At the snap, McKinney opened to his deep quarter, but with no vertical threat from any inside receiver, he was free to read the quarterback.

Maye finished his drop looking to the front side, then came back to the backside dig, with his head and shoulders turned before the ball came out. McKinney read the turn and drove downhill and inside, from deep-quarter depth to the spot where the dig would be caught, before Maye released it.

The throw was on time, but McKinney jumped into the throwing lane and caught it in front of Raridon at the 29. In quarters, a safety whose inside receiver doesn't go vertical can become a robber on in-breaking routes. Throwing a dig that late at that safety without a vertical route to hold him is exactly the throw the coverage is built to take away.

On these interceptions, the Packers only rushed three, four and four, and didn't get any pressure on Maye, who had time and threw every one of these picks from a clean pocket. Each pick came after the snap, when a Packers safety ended up somewhere Maye didn't expect.

McKinney stayed in the middle instead of biting on play action, Evan Williams rotated over the top of a one-on-one that wasn't, and McKinney turned a deep-quarter alignment into a robber on the dig. That's Jonathan Gannon's defense in a nutshell: show one picture, play another, and trust the safeties to beat the quarterback to the spot.

With Micah Parsons out and the injury list growing, Green Bay can't count on getting home with four. It doesn't have to when McKinney and Williams are this far ahead of the quarterback. Every passer left on the schedule will see the same disguises on film, and recognizing them on tape is a lot easier than beating them on Sunday.

#2844. Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance—2 habits that take 'a few seconds' can help you avoid similar traps

The biggest heist in cryptocurrency history began with small mistakes many internet users make. A hacking group tied to North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance. The operation was sophisticated, involving fake job interviews and malicious code.

But it was also mundane. Although artificial intelligence played a role in the hack, this was not a cyberattack of the future, propelled by swarms of AI agents. Rather, it relied on humans who made some basic errors, like clicking a link because it appeared first on a search results page or trusting strangers at a fake company without taking a few seconds to look them up.

We work at the Digital Inquiry Group, a nonprofit that researches how people evaluate online information and creates free, evidence-based curriculum that helps people decide what to trust.

In over a decade of research, we've found that people frequently engage in online behavior that makes them more likely to get duped. Two simple strategies can help you better navigate today's information landscape, from traditional phishing to misleading social posts to AI fakes. Here's how.

The Binance heist began when one of the company's engineers downloaded compromised software. That engineer, according to the Reuters investigation of the hack, clicked on a sponsored search result that appeared higher on the results page and directed them to the malicious code.

Our research at the Digital Inquiry Group suggests internet users frequently behave as if first is best. They click on the first thing they see. They incorrectly associate a higher placement with vetted content, ceding judgment to tech company algorithms. Students have gone so far as to tell us "Google is almost never wrong" or "AI is always right."

Professional fact-checkers commonly practice click restraint. They understand that whether you're searching on the internet or querying a chatbot, first isn't always best. If you're researching an organization, the first link will often be to its own site, which is hardly likely to disclose anything that's wrong with it.

So the next time you search for something online, be wary of links to sponsored content, the organization you're investigating, or to open platforms where anyone can post and information isn't verified, such as Quora or Reddit. Read the brief snippets beneath each link, and make a more informed choice about what to open.

Always ask yourself: Who is behind this information? What makes them credible? Look for people and organizations that have direct expertise on the topic at hand, or have processes to ensure the accuracy of information, such as news outlets that employ editors and fact-checkers.

Binance says it caught that first malicious download, replaced the device and changed passwords. But later, another engineer downloaded compromised code as part of what they thought was a job interview, which included a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fake company.

It's tempting to think that the engineer should have seen something was off. But the internet is a precarious place because bad actors know how to make content feel legitimate. Binance says its employee was snared by a hacker posing as an HR rep who "shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust."

When they encounter a piece of unfamiliar content, professional fact-checkers don't just read it closely — they read laterally. They open new browser tabs to see what other, credible sources have to say. Fact-checkers know that bad actors make themselves look good on their home turf, but that it's a lot harder to fake a good reputation across the internet.

The next time you encounter something unfamiliar online, look for authoritative sources that can shed light on the person or organization. You might find a news article that confirms the claim you're looking into, or a report that identifies a supposedly neutral source as biased.

In some cases, you may find nothing at all, which is a signal in itself: if you look up a company that reached out to you and find no external confirmation of its existence, that should be an immediate red flag.

Had that first Binance engineer engaged in click restraint and verified the source of the software, they might have avoided the malicious download. Had that second employee taken time to seek external verification about the supposed HR rep, rather than trusting a polished social media profile, they might have realized that something didn't add up.

The internet and AI have made it harder to know whether what we see is authentic. They've also made it easier than ever before to investigate who or what we encounter online. It's always worth pausing to check. A few seconds up front can save us all a lot of time, grief and money later on.

Nadav Ziv is a researcher at the Digital Inquiry Group. Joel Breakstone is co-founder and executive director of the Digital Inquiry Group.

#2843. Sam Hartman NFL contract: What the new 'Bachelor' earns with Commanders

For the second time ever, "The Bachelor" is going to be an active NFL player.

Washington Commanders quarterback Sam Hartman has been named the new star for Season 30 of ABC's reality dating franchise. The 27-year-old admitted during an appearance on "Good Morning America" it was the previous NFL player to serve as "Bachelor" who helped convince him to hand out roses to 30 women seeking a romantic relationship on national television.

Jesse Palmer, who was named the host of "The Bachelor" in 2021, was a member of the New York Giants when he starred on the show. Palmer ended the season in a relationship with winner Jessica Bowlin, but they split a month after the May 2004 finale.

"He kind of gave me the insight, what it is, what it's not," Hartman said of Palmer. "I'm excited but also very nervous."

Palmer appeared in eight NFL games during his career, though none came after his stint as "The Bachelor." Hartman has mainly been on Washington's practice squad during his three NFL seasons.

Here's a closer look at Hartman's Commanders contract, how NFL practice squads work and his NFL career to date.

NFL HOT SEAT RANKINGS: Coaches most likely to be fired

Hartman was part of the Commander's final preseason roster cuts in August 2026 and then re-signed to the team's practice squad for the third-straight year. He is to set to make $247,500 in base salary if he remains with Washington's practice squad for the entire 2026 NFL season based on the league's collective bargaining agreement.

Experience determines how much money a practice squad player can make.

Those with more than two seasons of experience can negotiate contracts with a salary range between $18,350 and $22,850 per week, according to the NFL's collective bargaining agreement. That equates to a salary between $330,300 and $411,300 if a player were to remain on a team's practice squad for the entire season. Players with fewer than two seasons will make $13,750 per week in 2026, or $247,500 for the entire season.

Hartman falls into the latter category because he has yet to appear in an NFL game. Contracts for players on the practice squad do not count towards an NFL team's salary cap.

"The Bachelor" Season 30 with Sam Hartman will premiere March 21, 2027, at 8 p.m. ET/PT on ABC.

Hartman began his professional career in 2024 after playing his final collegiate season at Notre Dame in 2023. He also played five seasons at Wake Forest and went undrafted in the 2024 NFL Draft. But Hartman signed with the Commanders as a free agent.

Hartman was part of the active roster for the first five games of the 2024 season and the final two games of the 2025 season without appearing in a game. He also started Washington's first preseason game in August against the New England Patriots.

During the 2026 season, Hartman is Washington's fourth-string quarterback behind starter Jayden Daniels, backup Marcus Mariota and rookie third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis.

#2842. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users

OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.

The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.

OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.

"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts.

Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.

OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an "Instant Checkout" feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.

Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.

"We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said.

OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.

"It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview.

Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.

OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.

"It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants."

#2841. Did USC football team fly to Indiana before nationwide ground stop?

USC football will need its air attack to be effective against the Indiana Hoosiers, but before the game starts, the Trojans need to get to the game site. You might be wondering if USC's team plane left Los Angeles before the nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday. USA TODAY has updates. So does Chris Vannini of The Athletic.

Vannini reports that USC's plane did leave LA before the ground stop, so USC-Indiana will go on as scheduled on Saturday. Other teams weren't as lucky, and it raises real questions about Saturday's college football schedule. This has become a nationwide story given that the ground stop has nationwide reach. The USC-Indiana game is scheduled for a mid-afternoon kickoff in Bloomington, Indiana, at 3:30 p.m. Eastern time on CBS. That's 12:30 p.m. Pacific time. Had USC not gotten off the ground before the stop, this game might have been subject to a reschedule and a night kickoff to accommodate a later arrival by the visiting team.

Texas did not get off the ground before the stop. The "USC Bowl" between Steve Sarkisian and Lane Kiffin now has another plot point to account for. That game is a scheduled night game, so Horns-Tigers might not be delayed.

Minnesota didn't get out before the ground stop, but the Gophers' game at Penn State is also a night game, so it might not be rescheduled.

This one is interesting. Tennessee did not get out of Knoxville before the ground stop. This game is scheduled for a 3 p.m. Eastern, 2 p.m. local time kickoff on Saturday. This game could get shoved several hours back into a night slot in College Station, Texas.

Ole Miss did not get out of Oxford before the ground stop. This is a 4:15 p.m. Eastern, 3:15 p.m. local time kickoff in Norman, Oklahoma (Central time zone). This game might be pushed back, too.

This is a 1:30 p.m. local kick from Provo in the Mountain time zone. This game could be moved into a night slot. Remember that BYU can't play on Sundays, either, so the Big 12 will want to get this game in by Saturday night.

This is a 3:30 p.m. kickoff in Orlando on Saturday. Arizona State has a long plane flight to deal with, from Tempe (or Phoenix) to Orlando. This game could easily be moved back several hours.

Michigan made it to Oregon. Northwestern made it to Ohio State. Washington did not yet get to East Lansing for the Michigan State game. Purdue will take a bus to get to Iowa City for the game against the Iowa Hawkeyes. Nebraska's plane left before the ground stop and will make it to Rutgers in New Jersey. Illinois plays UCLA Friday night, so the Illini had no problem getting to Los Angeles.

#2839. Joel Embiid’s aggressiveness was a welcome sight for Sixers

The Sixers losing two out of three games wasn't necessarily cause for much concern, but the way they lost those games raised some alarm bells. Particularly with Joel Embiid, who has yet to find his shot this season. His defense also began to deteriorate over the past couple of games as he dealt with plantar fasciitis in his right foot.

Through his first 10 games of the season, Embiid shot just 37% from the field and a career-low 55% from the rim. That included a game where he went 0-for-9 from the field in Cleveland against the Cavaliers, one of the worst performances of his career.

After being blown out by the Boston Celtics, Embiid admitted that he might be in his own head.

"[I'm] probably overthinking it too much," he said, "and then I think the rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different."

The Toronto Raptors coming to town provided a good opportunity for a get-right game. Not only were they down multiple key starters and on the second night of a back-to-back, but their starting center, Jakob Poeltl, has struggled mightily all season.

Embiid didn't completely snap out of his funk. His 20 points came on 7-of-17 shooting. Toronto was able to get into the lane with relative ease all night, but anyone watching the game could tell that Embiid was moving around the floor much better than he had in recent outings as the Sixers got back in the win column. That fact was capped off by Embiid dunking not once but twice.

"I think it's a really, really big positive," said head coach Nick Nurse. "I think that he's just moving better, and I'm not sure that was the case for a couple games here recently."

Embiid was able to do all of this after scaring every Sixers fan at the beginning of the game. Early in the first quarter he bumped knees with Ja'Kobe Walter as he was setting a screen and went down in a heap of pain. He went back to the locker room but was able to return three minutes later of game time.

Nurse said that Embiid was "very, very motivated" to play once he had returned to the locker room — so much so that Nurse had trouble subbing him out for his scheduled rests. Nurse did say that's a good problem, sometimes.

Embiid didn't talk after the game, but he told reporters at shootaround before the game that he needed to be more aggressive. While he still didn't hit as many midrange jumpers as he's used to, that aggression was visible in his shot selection — 10 of his 17 attempts came from the paint and it looked like he really started to hunt dunks. He nearly had another self-lob off the backboard, but Collin Murray-Boyles got in the way, forcing Embiid to kick the ball out to Kentavious Caldwell-Pope for a three.

"It's nice to see the kind of movement spark come back," Nurse said. "You've heard me say this a lot too. When he's driving the ball, he's feeling pretty good."

There's still a ways to go for Embiid getting back on track. That lethal jumper he's so famous for still has to come around. At the same time, the aggression he showed in attacking the basket was a welcome sight for every Sixer.

"I always tell him, 'Bro, like you're the MVP of this league,'" VJ Edgecombe said, "you're that good, you're that good.' I always tell him, 'No one can stop you. There's not one person in the NBA than can guard you.'"

If this is the start of Embiid putting it together, the Sixers' offense can finally start to look as dangerous as it was advertised over the summer. The fact that they've started the season 10-3 in the mean time is one hell of a cushion.

#2837. They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'

Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flattering message on LinkedIn just complimenting your background and your profile and your experience."

"Every hand goes up," she says. Then, she tells attendees how responding to a simple adulatory message could unwittingly open the door to a potential romance scam.

Delaney is a corporate security expert, well-versed in teaching people how to avoid “honeypot” schemes, in which a bad actor uses romantic or sexual interest to build trust and gain information, access or leverage over a target. The term is currently making headlines in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation from the company, following reporting on his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Honeypots, also known as "honey traps," are a very human form of social engineering attack, a category that also includes various forms of phishing and use of deepfake technology. And you don't have to be a billionaire tech CEO to possess information that scammers may value.

As competition in the global artificial intelligence race heats up, OpenAI is reportedly training employees to recognize espionage tactics including bribery, romantic manipulation and blackmail, according to The Wall Street Journal. On Nov. 3, cryptocurrency exchange Binance revealed that a recent cyberattack — which saw roughly $6 billion of digital assets stolen — was partially made possible by a fake job interview scheme that infected an employee’s work computer with malware.

"People can get solicited, bribed, romanced, etc.," says Kevin Tian, co-founder and CEO of Doppel, an AI-powered platform meant to help identify and deflect social engineering attacks. He adds: "If you've got access to sensitive IP [intellectual property] — it's not just AI companies — you can be a target."

Increasingly, scammers can use AI to scour websites ranging from Reddit to Pinterest for an individual's personal information and customize a ploy designed specifically for them, Tian says. Once they have relevant data points, attackers tend to use "the oldest tricks in the book: elicitation, flattery, ego," says Delaney, a former intelligence officer with the Defense Intelligence Agency and the founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based corporate security consulting firm Vaillance Group.

In many cases, Delaney notes, targets have an inkling that something is suspicious — but they'd rather allow themselves to believe the interest is legitimate. So how do you keep yourself from falling victim? Trust your self-awareness, common sense and ability to identify situations that feel too good to be true, she says.

"The bottom line is, we're all human," says Delaney, adding: "It feels so good to be wanted, or to be respected, or to be appreciated, or loved."

Delaney, who has worked with Fortune 500 companies such as Uber and Merck, advises corporate clients on cybersecurity risks and develops training programs to improve employees' awareness of security threats. Her sessions aim to build awareness of manipulative connections, such as romance scams, from how they begin to the natural progression they often take. "Introduction, then repeated contact, favors, sensitive requests — the secrecy, the pressure," she says.

Bad actors may tap into any information you post online to find an interest that can be mirrored and exploited, or an acquaintance who can be infiltrated and make an introduction. If someone you know and trust makes an introduction, you might be less likely to "go do due diligence" on the new person, even if they're a stranger, Delaney says.

One of Vaillance's services includes building a "targeting package" around an executive or C-Suite member, says Delaney. "We can show how they are vulnerable and how we would target that organization just by leveraging the people around them in that circle: spouses, friends, kids, parents, administrative assistants, neighbors," she says. "That's when people's eyes open."

From there, she discusses red flags to spot. Conversations that begin with flattery and seemingly innocuous small talk can gradually shift toward digging for information, introductions to colleagues or access to documents, says Delaney. It's human nature to want to be helpful and fulfill friendly requests, she adds. Add a potential romantic connection to the mix, especially amid an ongoing "loneliness epidemic," and the urge to comply can be even harder to resist, she says.

If you feel yourself getting cornered in a situation where a recent acquaintance or romantic partner keeps asking for information you're not comfortable revealing, Delaney says it helps to have first practiced polite refusal. "One of my favorites is: They could just respond with: 'Why do you ask?'" she says. "Put the other person on the defensive. You could give a nondescript answer. You can say you don't know. You can say you can't respond."

If you're ever suspicious of a new connection — even if you don't want to be — do yourself a favor and conduct some basic vetting, she recommends. You might examine their social media profiles and other publicly available information, for example, to see if their story checks out.

If you can't find enough information to allay your suspicions, don't be shy about alerting your employer's security or human resources team, she says. For smaller companies, or scams outside the workplace, you can file a complaint for cyber threats or romance scams with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center.

And pay attention if your new paramour starts asking you specific questions about your finances or work credentials, says Delaney.

"If you have no game at home, and you get off an airplane somewhere and suddenly everyone's all over you, we call that a red flag," she says.

#2836. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

#2835. Fantasy football Week 10 streamers: Who can save your lineup from bye weeks?

Post-NFL trade deadline, four teams on bye weeks, and the push for the fantasy playoffs is upon us.

Let's look at 10 players who are widely available and who you can stream in Week 10 if your lineup is in need of help.

(Streamers are players who are rostered in 50% or fewer of Yahoo leagues.)

Among quarterbacks with at least 50 dropbacks, Lock leads the league with 0.33 EPA/play. Of course, it's a much smaller sample size for him overall, but he's performing well so far, and that should continue against the Las Vegas Raiders. In three games this season (two starts), he's posted 12.7, 21.4 and 12.6 fantasy points. They're not massive numbers, but with the Raiders allowing the third-most fantasy points to quarterbacks (20.4), Lock is in another good spot.

With an over/under total of 49.5 points, we have to consider options from this game for streaming. The Steelers are coming off their bye week and face a Bengals defense that has allowed 17.3 points per game to quarterbacks. Rodgers put that on full display in Week 3 when he posted 23.68 fantasy points with 292 yards, three touchdowns and one interception, which was a huge showing. That's certainly his ceiling, but seeing 14-18 points from Rodgers as a streamer is very viable at this point in the season.

Estime played on 47% of the snaps last week compared to 49% for Alvin Kamara, but Estime is the option you want. Kamara only posted 7.9 PPR points on nine touches, while Estime posted 14.7 on 16 touches. Estime out-carried Kamara 15-6. It's an elite matchup for Estime, since the Carolina Panthers have allowed a whopping 27.6 PPR fantasy points to running backs, which is the second-most in the NFL. With D'Andre Swift, Saquon Barkley, Bucky Irving and Jonah Coleman all on bye weeks, Estime is a solid streaming option this week.

Johnson stepped in last week to lead the team with 14 carries for 68 yards and a touchdown after Jacobs went out with a finger injury. While MarShawn Lloyd is expected back this week, he's been largely ineffective overall, posting more than 10.0 PPR points just one time this season. Johnson doesn't have any pass-catching upside, but in a huge divisional matchup, seeing the Packers commit to the run game against the Vikings' defense shouldn't come as a shock. We saw James Cook on the Bills have success last week, providing a blueprint for the Packers.

With George Pickens still listed as questionable, Flournoy could be in for another starting role opposite CeeDee Lamb. While Flournoy had that role last week and ended with only 7.3 PPR points, he played on a season-high 97% of the offensive snaps and ran 38 routes, which was tied with Lamb. It's certainly a tougher matchup against the San Francisco 49ers' defense, but the role and playing time are there, which can't be said about all streamers in the free agent pool.

I know the Chargers don't inspire any confidence, but with four teams on bye weeks there are several normal starting wide receivers that aren't available this week. Ladd McConkey wasn't able to go last week and it allowed Johnston to post his best game of the season with 12.80 PPR points. The Ravens allow the 11th-most PPR points per game (34.0) to wide receivers, making this a decent matchup for Johnston if your league is deep and you are desperate for a starter.

Matthew Stafford has to throw the ball to someone, right? Davante Adams is still out, and Puka Nacua is now out. That makes Atwell and Konata Mumpfield the two starting wide receivers. Some people might have forgotten that the Rams reacquired Atwell at the end of August after he signed with the Miami Dolphins during the offseason. Last week, Atwell played on 47% of the snaps, ran 25 routes and saw five targets. Those numbers don't jump off the page, but Nacua did play last week. Atwell has some experience with Stafford, and this matchup against the Arizona Cardinals is too good to pass up.

#2834. The Grizzlies are way ahead of schedule, but still have a long way to go

Every season comes with its own unique twists and turns. If it wasn't that way, all of our offseason prediction pieces would be perfect and there would be no point in playing any games.

Fortunately, this year has been no different. Chief among all the unexpected outcomes are the Memphis Grizzlies, who, in what was supposed to be the first year of a rebuild, sit at 7-4 with the 10th-best net-rating in the entire association.

With teams like the Oklahoma City Thunder and Minnesota Timberwolves enduring significant injuries, and others like the Denver Nuggets looking too old for their own good, it is plausible that the West is more wide-open than we initially believed. But is it possible for the Grizzlies to be this ahead of schedule? Or is this just a flash of what they will eventually become?

It feels cliche to say this given how much this team has permeated the NBA zeitgeist since they won it all, but this Grizzlies group really does resemble the 2013-14 Beautiful Game San Antonio Spurs.

The Spurs were an incredibly deep team that reached the Platonic ideals for decision-making speed, spacing, and ball movement. Head coach Tuomas Iisalo has the Grizzlies on this current trajectory.

Iisalo basically load manages his team to ensure that they are as fresh as possible. This year, 13 Grizzlies have played at least 70 total minutes. The only other teams that can say that are the Indiana Pacers, Golden State Warriors, Oklahoma City Thunder, and Utah Jazz  – all of whom have had to deal with their fair share of injuries. So, their digging deep into their bench is more out of necessity than it is a tactical decision.

Under this new regime, the Grizzlies are deploying a multi-layered, ball-screen continuity attack predicated around the pick-and-roll and side-to-side ball movement. Iisalo quite literally refers to the concept as "flow," which is poetic considering the way the offense softly cascades from action to action. The intricacies of their futuristic style are outside of the scope of the current discussion, but if you want to learn more, be sure to check out this deep dive from Coach Gibson Pyper:

As any coach will tell you, strategy will only take you so far. You need the players who can execute your vision or else it doesn't matter how smart you are. This offense requires skilled operates (Ty Jerome and Cam Spencer), strong screeners (Zach Edey, Cam Boozer, and Isaiah Stewart), shooters/closeout attackers (Cedric Coward, Jaylen Wells, Jerami Grant, and Quentin Post), and speedy court mappers (Boozer may be better than any rookie at this in all of NBA history).

The bottom line is that this team has a litany of legit players. This also shows on the defensive side of the ball, where the Grizzlies currently rank fifth (just like on offense). It starts in the middle. Prior to the start of the season, I called Stewart one of the best defensive bigs in the league, and the only thing stopping me from doing the same with Edey were his lingering injury concerns. Edey, in particular, is looking like a fringe Defensive Player of the Year candidate. When he's out there, the Grizzlies are in the 99th percentile in defensive rating (per Cleaning the Glass). That's in a league that features Victor Wembanyama. Between him and Stewart, that's an excellent defensive foundation.

Wells and Coward are a pair of rangy wings, with powers that perfectly compliment each other (Wells is better at defending the ball, Coward has more of a presence off-ball). Grant and GG Jackson have size and length. Boozer moves better than anyone with his muscle mass should reasonably be expected to. Kris Murray would get more buzz for his defensive prowess if his offense wasn't so damaging.

Iisalo's theory about keeping bodies fresh has come to fruition. While many teams are operating at half-speed, conserving themselves for the 82-game grind, the Grizzlies are moving like it's the first round of the postseason. An abundance of youthful vigor (the Grizzlies are the third-youngest team in the league) certainly helps, too. Look at the way Wells and Boozer are sliding their feet in this first clip, or the diligence from Spencer to x-out and kill the advantage created by Braden Smith:

If you're a fan of the team or in any way affiliated with the organization, you should feel very excited about what you are building. Boozer, Coward, Edey, Wells, Jackson, and Stewart are all 25 years old and younger. The future is bright in Memphis, but for right now, there are some indicators that tell us negative regression is coming.

The Grizzlies are second in 3-point percentage and eighth opponent 3-point percentage. Opponent 3-point percentage is almost exclusively contingent on variables outside of a defense's control, and, on the flip side, I doubt this group will remain the second-best shooting team in the association for the entirety of the marathon.

Dunks & Threes has a metric which ranks a team's strength of schedule from the games they've already played (SOS). According to that, the Grizzlies have had the second-easiest schedule this year, with their best win coming against a Warriors team that had yet to hit its stride.

In their recent loss against the Indiana Pacers, we got front row seats at their biggest shortfall: guard play/ball handling. Outside of Ty Jerome, Cam Spencer, and Scottie Pippen Jr. (who is hurt right now), the Grizzlies don't have much in terms of pressure breakers, and none of those three gentlemen is a black belt in this art form. The Pacers' token fullcourt pressure hounded the Grizzlies all night, to the tune of 20 turnovers and their lowest offensive rating output of the season.

This could be remedied if Iisalo started playing two of these three together more frequently, but in that case, it would weaken their formidability on the other side of the ball. Patching up one whole leads to another. A telltale sign of a flawed unit.

If I was a prospective general manager, who could pick a ten-year gig with any team in the league, it would take one hand to count off the places I'd pick over the Grizzlies. What they have here is real, and it seems more bulletproof than the last generation (no pun intended, I swear). But right now, in 2026-27, I find it difficult to see the Grizzlies as anything more than a fringe playoff team.

#2832. Supreme Court agrees to hear Robinhood challenge to IPO information omission lawsuit

The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case in which Robinhood seeks to block a class-action lawsuit over the omission of interim financial data from the online broker's initial public offering in 2021.

Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities.

A San Francisco federal court judge had previously dismissed the lawsuit.

The Trump administration and the Securities and Exchange Commission had urged the Supreme Court to hear Robinhood's appeal.

"We are pleased the Supreme Court has agreed to hear our case and look forward to presenting our argument," a Robinhood spokesperson said in a statement.

CNBC has requested comment from the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the case.

Robinhood's IPO came on the heels of a surge in investor interest during the Covid-19 pandemic in so-called meme stocks, and trading in the crypto asset dogecoin.

In July 2021, Robinhood conducted its IPO, "for which it prepared a registration statement" that "contained only limited information about Robinhood's performance during the second quarter of 2021," the 9th Circuit panel that heard the case noted.

"After the initial public offering, Robinhood reported financial results from that second quarter, and its stock price dropped," the panel wrote.

The investors who sued Robinhood and the other defendants alleged the registration statement omitted material information it was legally required to disclose.

#2830. Ferguson 'made up' with first win as Glens boss

At the third time of asking, Duncan Ferguson is finally up and running as Glentoran manager.

After two draws to start his tenure in the Irish Premiership, a home debut for the former Everton striker had late drama under the Friday night lights at the Oval.

Jordan Stewart, dubbed the "wee man" by big Dunc after his first game, celebrated his contract extension by scoring the opening goal and, in a largely uneventful game, it looked like that would be the difference.

However, that all changed when Ben Cushnie equalised for Bangor in the 83rd minute, but there was more drama to follow as Cal Weatherup raced onto a long ball to slot home the winner with three minutes remaining and secure a first win for Ferguson as boss.

"I'm delighted to get my first three points at home, I'm absolutely made up," Ferguson said after the game.

"The boys kept on going until the very end."

Weatherup's late goal gives Ferguson first Glens win

Ferguson's first game in the Irish League was meant to be at home to Ballymena United on 24 October, but Storm Boelo and a waterlogged pitch delayed his highly-anticipated debut in the league.

Stewart scored the equaliser at then-leaders Coleraine in his first outing in the dugout the following week, and the Glens were then held to a goalless draw at Carrick Rangers.

But on Friday, Ferguson finally announced himself to the home support in east Belfast.

Despite a controlled first half and Stewart's opener, Ferguson felt that his side "sat too deep" before Bangor's equaliser, which came through former Glentoran man Cushnie.

But it was teenager Weatherup who was ultimately the difference, with a finish that Ferguson would have been proud of in his playing days as he slotted the ball between the legs of the onrushing Patrick Solis Grogan for his first goal of the campaign.

Ferguson said he was "made up" for the 18-year-old, who replaced Pat Hoban midway through the second half.

"We showed good character. We showed a bit of resilience," added the 54-year-old.

"They put us under pressure in the second half but that will happen. You're not going to dominate a game for the whole game at any level.

"I was delighted the boys showed character and resilience to get back into the game."

Given their mixed start to the season, a charge at the Irish Premiership title is going to be a long shot.

But if the Glens are to have any aspirations of a first Gibson Cup since 2009 then it is important for them to keep pace with those above.

Leaders Linfield and nearest challengers Coleraine both were comfortable winners on Friday, while Larne bounced back from their poor recent win to beat Dungannon Swifts.

Glentoran are 14 points off the Blues but have a game in hand, and they face another tricky home test against Cliftonville next Friday to try and build upon the win over the Seasiders.

As he reflected on his start to the league, Ferguson admitted "I think we need to get better overall.

"We're not conceding many goals, but we just have to create more.

"That's the hardest part of the game, but we look solid and that's the main thing.

"I'm happy with the group and the league is very close together, from top to bottom".

With that in mind, especially as he continues his early steps in the league, it's just "one game at a time" for Ferguson, rather than thinking too far ahead.

"We've just got to keep going. I think that is seven or eight games undefeated now," he added.

"We have to keep going and keep winning. We're a big club and the fans want us to keep winning, and I'm glad we got the three points for them today."

#2828. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years

Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.

The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.

Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.

On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.

The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.

Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.

Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.

The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.

However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.

"Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.

Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.

"We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."

Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.

Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.

Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.

"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."

Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

#2826. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. #2825. After Jensen Huang’s exit, what top financial advisors are doing with Nvidia: Exclusive CNBC poll

Shares of Nvidia continued to slide after the market open on Friday after declining 4% on Thursday following news of co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, amid reports about his personal relationships and national security concerns. The news has raised questions for investors about what comes next for a company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom.

To gauge how wealth managers are responding, CNBC polled members of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council. Thirty of the 122 firms and professionals contacted responded to the online, multiple-choice flash poll, conducted between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. EST on Nov. 12. The poll is a snapshot of respondents' views, not a measure of all financial advisors.

Most respondents, 19, said they are holding their Nvidia positions steady. Another four said they are increasing their stake, while seven said they do not own the stock. None said they were selling at the time of the poll.

"Most of our clients are in a position to hold; the reason is because it makes up a smaller percentage of an overall diversified portfolio," Winnie Sun, managing director and founding partner of Irvine, California-based Sun Group Wealth Partners, said in an interview. Sun is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council.

Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:

In open responses, several advisors wrote that they are taking a "wait-and-see" approach before changing their investment strategy with Nvidia and are telling their clients to do the same.

"Don't react to short-term headlines," wrote certified financial planner Peyton Jamison, president of Jamison Private Wealth Management in Alpharetta, Georgia. "The company's valuation is extremely attractive, and the focus should remain on its underlying fundamentals and long-term investment potential." His firm is ranked No. 78 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.

Asked what factors could change their approach to Nvidia, 13 respondents cited the outlook for AI demand, 11 pointed to valuation, and 10 mentioned company leadership or governance. Some said the decision depends on the client, with eight citing risk tolerance and seven mentioning portfolio concentration. Seven said they do not expect to change their approach.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results Tuesday, after the market close. In poll remarks, advisors said the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings will help determine their course of action.

Advisors said that for investors, what to do may depend on how much Nvidia stock they already own, when they expect to need the money and how comfortable they are with volatility.

"If this is a company that's going to keep you up at night and you just feel really uncomfortable with these unknown risks, then there was always the option to sell and move that capital to another stock or another portfolio," Sun said.

Nvidia exposure can also come through mutual funds and ETFs. Nvidia's large market value makes it a significant holding in many broad-market funds, including funds that track the S&P 500, as well as target-date funds in retirement-plan options.

Investors can check their Nvidia exposure by reviewing the fact sheets for the funds in their 401(k) or brokerage accounts, which typically list a fund's largest holdings. A stock's decline does not translate one-for-one into a fund's decline.

However, investors with dedicated technology, semiconductor or growth funds may have more Nvidia exposure than they realize, advisors say.

"Nvidia is a big part of virtually everyone's portfolio whether they take an active or passive index approach," wrote Andy Pratt, a partner and director of investment strategy at Burney Wealth Management in Reston, Virginia, which is ranked No. 34 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list.

He said he advises clients not to overreact to short-term news and to let the dust settle before making decisions.

— CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

#2823. Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker

In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.

The Wall Street firm liked what it heard.

"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.

Yet the firm formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.

The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, according to Axios.

By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to Axios, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.

Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.

Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.

An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.

Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."

"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.

There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.

"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.

Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick and his sons did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.

As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.

Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.

But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the Departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."

Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."

Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy. At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing.

That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing, as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China.

Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026, with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.

Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.

"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to non-public government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.

The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.

Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30, the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.

Cantor has not publicly explained the decline.

Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured, a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.

As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to Axios, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show.

On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.

"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.

Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.

Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, Axios reported.

On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs.

On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.

It is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.

Still, Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.

By the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.

Cantor didn't answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.

IREN was not the only company in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.

In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle.

Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor, also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.

Ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium, which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.

It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.

Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.

In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick announced the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false."

TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.

Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from his push to expand AI data centers.

And on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons, D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.

The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."

"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.
